On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

items.title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
items.author: Yifan Cai, Linh Thi Xuan Phan
items.content: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($\epsilon=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.

items.title: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
items.author: Wenzhuo Xu, Zonghao Ying, Deyue Zhang, Dongdong Yang, Xiangzheng Zhang, Quanchen Zou
items.content: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce \textbf{Detail Guidance Attack (DGA)}, a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.

items.title: TailGuard-GDS: Tail-Safe Control of GPU Storage Data Movement
items.author: Jiaqi Liu, Fan Yang, Xiaohang Shi, Xianzhe Zhang, Tao Jiang, Guojun Yuan, Zhan Wang, Guangming Tan
items.content: AI runtimes move state between NVMe storage and GPU memory on critical paths. GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes host staging, yet our eight-H100 measurements show it is not consistently tail-optimal for semantically identical GPU-buffer operations. The preferred path varies with operation, request size, concurrency, placement, and resource contention; bandwidth and tail-latency winners can disagree. Frameworks specify what moves and when, while GPU I/O stacks expose mechanisms; neither combines phase semantics with measured tail behavior to choose a delivery plan. We present TailGuard-GDS, a runtime that selects a semantically equivalent plan per application phase. It profiles plans varying backend, request shape, and placement, minimizes GPU-visible tail latency under phase constraints, and revisits decisions as conditions change. Resource reuse keeps policy lookup and switching at microsecond-scale overhead. Integrated with PyTorch FSDP and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, TailGuard reduces FSDP step p95 by 18.4% and GPU-idle p95 by 25.3% versus the strongest fixed path. Across five eight-GPU ZeRO-3 workloads, step p95 falls 7.9-24.6% versus fixed host staging and 28.4-42.6% versus fixed GDS. Against tuned DeepSpeed AIO, TailGuard reduces step p95 by 5.6% and raises estimated throughput by 6.1%.

items.title: OrbitWeaver: LLM Agent Planning with Simulation Feedback for Optically Interconnected Orbital GPU Clusters
items.author: Pengcheng Luo, Bowen Zhang
items.content: Space-based data-center designs increasingly consider GPU computing formations connected by inter-satellite optical links. With limited neighboring connections, jobs assigned disjoint GPUs can still contend on shared relay paths. Rank placement and communication priorities jointly affect this contention and the readiness of downstream computation. We present OrbitWeaver, an offline large language model (LLM) agent planner that jointly optimizes rank placement and communication order. Guided by communication structure, execution dependencies, and simulation feedback, the agent constructs and refines plans that coordinate shared-link access with computation progress. This coordination reduces contention and dependency blocking, shortening mean job completion time (JCT). Simulation experiments on optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters show that OrbitWeaver reduces aggregate mean JCT by 6.2-33.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baselines CASSINI, Crux, and Symphony. These results demonstrate the value of LLM-guided planning for efficient concurrent computing in orbital GPU clusters.

items.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
items.author: Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Neil Gong
items.content: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.

items.title: RuralShield: Super Intelligence-Assisted Security Triage and Serverless Infrastructure for Resource-Constrained Healthcare
items.author: Mohammad Arman Ullah, Asif Ahmed
items.content: Resource-constrained healthcare providers must connect cloud security controls to an operational response process. Introducing language-model assessments adds an authorization problem: a recommendation must be converted into a permitted action against a specific resource. RuralShield combines a configurable serverless application foundation with structured model assessment, deterministic routing, and human-approved containment. Its design separates workload access, assessment validation, and action authorization so that each boundary produces inspectable records. We evaluate the implementation through a frozen 120-hour non-AI workload and separate desktop and AWS AI cohorts. The workload recorded 999,861 authenticated requests and 999,860 successful responses, with one HTTP 404 and one missing minute representing 139 scheduled requests. Median, 95th-percentile, and 99th-percentile Ohio client latencies were 28.57, 53.01, and 110.77 ms. Eight successful model requests exercised assessment and reporting in two four-case cohorts. The AWS cohort and five scripted controls produced nine completed workflows, including two human-approved Lambda containment cases with verified restoration of the original concurrency setting. Source-linked, checksum-verified archives preserved the records before scoped cleanup. The study demonstrates an inspectable integration of application controls and human-mediated AI response under the evaluated synthetic conditions.
